title: Counting clicks that arrive late
teaches: Event time and processing time, windows and watermarks, exactly-once effects by deduplication, and sketches for heavy hitters

blocks.text: An advertiser on Google's search pages pays when someone clicks the ad, so every click costs money. One server logs the click itself, and another server, perhaps in another datacentre, logged the search that showed the ad earlier. To bill the click, the system must find and join the two records. In June 2013, at the SIGMOD conference in New York, Rajagopal Ananthanarayanan and his colleagues described Photon, the system that performed that join continuously across datacentres for Google's advertising, so advertisers could see their spending within seconds instead of the next day.

The Photon authors report a load of millions of events a minute with an average end-to-end latency under 10 seconds.[^photon] The throughput and latency were not the hardest parts of the problem. The difficulty lay in the consistency and availability requirements set out before any design began. No click could be billed twice, no click could be lost, and the system had to keep running if an entire datacentre failed.

Photon's builders worked in an order worth copying, choosing to **define what a correct answer is** before building the pipeline. To count clicks per minute, an engineer must first answer three questions in writing. Does a click belong to the minute in which it happened, or the minute in which the pipeline processed it? When is a minute's count complete, given that some clicks will arrive late? And how does the pipeline handle a duplicate click? Engineers must make these choices for every streaming system, either deliberately during design or by accident in production.

Each event has two timestamps. Its **event time** is when the action occurred, such as when the user's finger touched the ad. Its **processing time** is when the pipeline ingested and handled the record. The skew between the two clocks is never zero and is often large. Servers ship logs in batches every few seconds; a phone in a tunnel buffers its events until it reconnects minutes or hours later; a datacentre cut off from the network for 20 minutes flushes 20 minutes of accumulated events at once when its connection returns.

A streaming pipeline aggregates events into **windows**, which are bounded slices of time that each hold a separate count. **Fixed** windows (also called tumbling windows) slice time into equal, non-overlapping intervals, such as one window per minute. **Sliding** windows overlap, such as a 5-minute window computed every 1 minute. **Session** windows group bursts of individual user activity and close after a set period of inactivity, such as 30 minutes of silence. You can define any of these window types using either clock.

Assigning windows by processing time is simple because the pipeline only reads its own local clock, and it is the wrong choice for billing. Suppose a datacentre's click logs are delayed for 20 minutes and then drain in 2 minutes. A processing-time count records 0 clicks per minute for 20 minutes followed by a traffic spike 10 times the normal rate. An advertiser with an hourly budget sees that budget exhausted in 2 minutes by clicks that actually happened earlier. Counting by event time places every click into the minute it actually occurred, though the pipeline can never be certain that all events for a given minute have arrived.

When aggregating by event time, the window for 12:00 to 12:01 is not guaranteed to be complete at 12:01, or even at 12:05, because a phone could still be offline in a tunnel holding a click timestamped 12:00:30. A pipeline must still decide when to emit a window's result, using a mechanism called a **watermark**. The watermark is a monotonically increasing timestamp that represents the pipeline's running estimate of event-time progress. A watermark of 12:01 means the system estimates that all events timestamped before 12:01 have arrived. When the watermark passes a window's end timestamp, the pipeline emits the window's result. Tyler Akidau and his colleagues at Google described watermarks in their paper on MillWheel (VLDB 2013) and formalised the model in the Dataflow paper (VLDB 2015), which Apache Beam and Apache Flink implement.[^watermark]

A watermark is usually a heuristic estimate, calculated from the oldest unacknowledged timestamps reported by data sources, or from a fixed offset rule such as assuming no event arrives more than 20 seconds late. When the estimate is wrong, an event arrives after the watermark has passed its window's end. The pipeline classifies this record as a **late** event, and the engineer must configure the system either to drop it or to emit an updated count for that window. In the figure below, we plot each click by its event time on the horizontal axis and its processing time on the vertical axis. A click on the diagonal, where the two timestamps are equal, arrived with zero latency; the vertical distance above the diagonal measures its arrival delay. The brown line represents the watermark, offset vertically from the diagonal by the watermark delay, and any click plotted above that line is late.

blocks.task: Find settings that end with every minute's count right, and play the clock to the end

blocks.text: If you set a 20-second watermark delay and drop late clicks, the pipeline emits each 1-minute window 20 seconds after the minute ends, and four of the five windows undercount by 1 click. Raising the watermark delay to 4 minutes captures every click in the initial output, and delays every window's output by 4 minutes. Keeping the 20-second watermark and emitting revisions achieves both low latency for the initial output and eventual accuracy, provided downstream consumers can handle updated records for past windows. Most production pipelines emit revisions up to a configured **allowed lateness** threshold, such as 1 hour or 1 day. Once the watermark passes the end of the window plus the allowed lateness, the pipeline purges the window's state from memory to bound storage costs, and either drops subsequent late arrivals or routes them to an offline batch correction job. You should configure allowed lateness by measuring the arrival delay distribution of your actual data and choosing a threshold that covers, say, the 99.99th percentile of events.

A billing pipeline must emit revisions to charge accurately; an operational dashboard showing clicks per minute can drop late events if it displays the drop rate; an alerting pipeline that pages an on-call engineer at night needs a low-latency first result and ignores later revisions. Engineers must choose the windowing and lateness behaviour based on how downstream systems use the output, before designing the pipeline.

In lesson 16, we built a log that guarantees **at-least-once** delivery. When a consumer crashes, a replacement starts reading from the last committed offset and processes the uncommitted tail of events a second time. The underlying network exhibits the same retry behaviour. When a client phone sends a click over HTTP and receives no acknowledgement, it cannot distinguish a dropped request packet from a dropped response packet, so it retries the request and occasionally writes duplicate records into the log. As we will prove in lesson 22, no network protocol over an unreliable channel can prevent duplicates entirely, meaning true exactly-once *delivery* is impossible.

A pipeline can still achieve **exactly-once effects**, meaning a click increments the billing counter only once regardless of how many times the network or log delivers it. Engineers use two mechanisms to achieve this. The first is to make the write operation **idempotent**, so repeating it leaves the state unchanged, such as assigning a value to a key rather than incrementing a counter. Writing the record "click 42 occurred on ad 7" to a database table keyed by click ID produces the same stored state whether executed once or ten times. The second mechanism is deduplication, where the pipeline maintains a state table of processed event IDs and filters out duplicates. Both approaches require the client source to generate a globally unique ID for each event before its first transmission attempt.

Photon took the second way, at the scale of datacentres. It ran the whole pipeline in two or more datacentres at once, each reading every click, so that losing one cost nothing. Before counting a click, a joiner had to claim the click's ID in the **IdRegistry**, a table of IDs counted in the last few days, replicated across datacentres with Paxos (lesson 11). Whichever joiner claimed first counted the click; every other claim was refused. Sizing such a registry is arithmetic: IDs a day times days kept. At 50,000 clicks a second that is 4.3 billion IDs a day, and three days of 16-byte IDs is about 200 GB before replication.

blocks.caption: One click transmitted twice, processed by joiners in two datacentres. Latencies are illustrative.
blocks.task: Play it with no registry, then with the ID registry

blocks.text: A cross-datacentre Paxos round trip takes tens of milliseconds. If a single Paxos group executed one consensus round per click sequentially, its throughput would bottleneck at a few dozen clicks per second, whereas Google's ad traffic generated tens of thousands of clicks per second. To reach the required throughput, Photon's registry servers batched concurrent ID registration requests arriving within a few milliseconds into a single Paxos transaction, and sharded the registry keyspace by click ID across many independent Paxos groups to parallelise the consensus rounds. One failure mode remains in this protocol. If a joiner registers a click ID in the IdRegistry and crashes before writing the joined output to the billing log, the click is never billed, yet its ID is marked as consumed in the registry. Photon resolved this by running a background scanner that identified registered IDs lacking corresponding output records and re-injected those clicks into the pipeline. Consequently, Photon's billing counts were never too high, could briefly undercount after a worker crash, and converged to the exact count shortly after.[^gap]

Some aggregation queries over a stream require too much memory to compute exact answers. Answering "Which 100 web pages received the most views today?" exactly requires maintaining an individual counter for every unique page visited, which across billions of URLs requires billions of counters in memory. Answering "How many distinct users visited the site today?" exactly requires storing the set of all unique user IDs seen so far. Instead of storing every key, you can use a probabilistic data structure called a **sketch** to compute approximate answers within a fixed, small memory footprint, with mathematically guaranteed error bounds chosen in advance.

The **count-min sketch** (Graham Cormode and S. Muthukrishnan, 2005) is a small table of counters: *d* rows of *w* each, and a different hash function for each row. Its size is set by two numbers chosen in advance: ε, the largest error allowed, as a share of all items counted, and δ, the chance of exceeding it. To count an item, add one to the counter its hash picks in every row. To estimate an item's count, look at its *d* counters and take the smallest. Each counter is shared by every item that hashes to it, so every counter is at least the item's true count, and the smallest is the one least crowded by other items. The estimate can be too high, never too low.

blocks.caption: A count-min sketch tracking 200,000 page views across 50,000 unique pages following a skewed Zipfian popularity distribution. Synthetic data. The two sliders adjust the number of counters per row, w, and the number of rows, d, for a total of w × d counters.
blocks.task: Find a sketch of at most 2,500 counters in all (w × d) that names the top ten pages correctly

blocks.text: The error depends on the width and the total count, not on how many distinct items there are. With *w* = *e*/ε counters a row (*e* ≈ 2.718) and *d* = ln(1/δ) rows, an estimate is at most ε times the total too high, except with chance δ. For error under 0.1% of all views, *w* is about 2,700; for δ = 1%, ln(100) ≈ 4.6, so five rows: 13,600 counters, about 54 KB, whether there are a thousand pages or a billion. A sketch also merges: two machines' sketches with the same hashes add counter by counter, so each machine can sketch its share of the stream and a final step sums them. To find the top pages, keep a small heap of the current leaders beside the sketch, and check each arriving page's estimate against the smallest in it.

Distinct counts have their own sketch, **HyperLogLog** (Philippe Flajolet and colleagues, 2007). It hashes each item, uses the first 11 bits of the hash to choose one of 2,048 buckets, and keeps in each bucket a 6-bit register holding the longest run of leading zero bits seen in the rest of the hash. Long runs are rare, so the longest runs say roughly how many distinct items went by. 2,048 registers of 6 bits is 1.5 KB, and it counts billions of distinct items to within about 2%, and HyperLogLogs merge as count-min sketches do.[^hll]

Early streaming systems were trusted for speed and not for accuracy, so many companies ran two pipelines over the same data: a stream for answers within seconds, and a nightly batch job (lesson 8's MapReduce) whose results replaced the stream's when they arrived. Nathan Marz called this the **lambda architecture**. It works, and it means writing every piece of logic twice, in two systems, and keeping them in agreement.

In 2014 Jay Kreps argued for one pipeline instead, sometimes called the **kappa architecture**. Keep the input in a log with long retention (lesson 16), and when the logic changes or a bug is fixed, start a second copy of the same streaming job from the oldest offset, let it catch up, and switch readers over to its output. Event-time windows, watermarks and deduplication by ID are what make that work: replaying last week through the stream gives the same counts as the live run's final answers, because the answer depends on when clicks happened, not when they were read. The one difference is clicks that arrived later than the allowed lateness. The log holds them in arrival order, so a replay meets them just as late and drops them too, unless it is given a longer allowed lateness; only a batch job that reads the whole day before answering counts every one.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on windows, watermarks and counting
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A datacentre's click logs are held up for 20 minutes, then drain in 2 minutes. Why should a billing pipeline count clicks by event time rather than processing time?
choices: By processing time the 20 minutes of clicks all land in two 1-minute windows, creating a traffic spike that never happened, while the preceding 20 minutes show zero clicks
By processing time the held-up clicks are dropped as duplicates, because they arrive with timestamps the pipeline has already passed
By event time the pipeline needs no watermark at all, because each click already carries the minute it belongs to
items.why: Processing time records when the pipeline ingested a click. Event time assigns each click to the minute it actually occurred, at the cost of requiring a watermark to estimate when all events for that minute have arrived.

items.ask: What does a watermark of 12:01 indicate?
choices: That the pipeline's local system clock reads 12:01
That the pipeline estimates every event timestamped before 12:01 has arrived, so windows ending at or before 12:01 can emit their results
That every event timestamped before 12:01 is guaranteed to have arrived, so any older event arriving later must be a network duplicate
items.why: A watermark is a heuristic estimate of progress in event time. Because network delays vary, the estimate can be wrong, requiring the pipeline to handle late events via drops or window revisions.

items.ask: A pipeline emits each 1-minute window 20 seconds after the minute ends and drops late clicks; its counts are often slightly low. Which configuration change gives fast initial results that converge to exact counts for every click arriving within 1 hour?
choices: Count by processing time instead, so that every click is counted in the minute it arrives and none can be late
Keep the 20-second watermark delay, emit updated window counts when late clicks arrive, and set the allowed lateness to 1 hour
Raise the watermark delay to 1 hour
items.why: Emitting revisions keeps the initial latency at 20 seconds and corrects the count as delayed data arrives, provided downstream readers can consume updated values. Raising the watermark delay to 1 hour adds 1 hour of latency to every window; counting by processing time assigns delayed clicks to the wrong minute.

items.ask: A client phone sends a click, receives no acknowledgement and sends it again. How does a streaming pipeline ensure the advertiser is billed only once?
choices: Turn off retries on the phone, so that each click can only ever be sent across the network a single time
Use a message log that guarantees exactly-once delivery, so the second copy is never handed to a consumer
Generate a unique ID for the click on the phone before sending, and increment the count only the first time that ID is registered in a shared state store
items.why: Disabling client retries causes data loss when packets drop, and exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is impossible. Deduplicating events against a registry using a client-generated unique ID, or performing an idempotent write keyed by that ID, achieves an exactly-once effect.

items.ask: A count-min sketch estimates that a web page was viewed 1,240 times. What can you conclude about its true view count?
choices: The true count is at most 1,240, and is likely close to 1,240 if the sketch array is wide enough relative to the total stream volume
The true count is at least 1,240, because other pages that share its counters can only have added to them
The true count is within 1% of 1,240 in either direction, regardless of the width of the sketch or the total volume of the stream
items.why: Each counter in the sketch holds the queried page's true view count plus increments from colliding keys that hashed to the same index. Consequently, every counter (including the minimum of the d counters) is greater than or equal to the true count. Increasing the row width w reduces hash collisions and shrinks this overestimation error.

items.ask: A web service running across 100 servers must report the number of distinct users per day, out of roughly 1 billion total users. Which architecture fits best?
choices: Each server streams every user ID it sees to one central machine, which inserts them all into an in-memory hash set
Each server maintains a local HyperLogLog sketch occupying a few kilobytes, and an aggregator merges the 100 sketches into one at the end of the day
Each server counts its own local distinct users exactly using a hash set, and an aggregator sums the 100 integer counts at the end of the day
items.why: A billion IDs in one set is gigabytes on one machine. Adding per-machine counts counts anyone seen by two machines twice. HyperLogLogs merge without double counting, within about 2%.

items.ask: A Photon joiner registers a click's ID in the Paxos-replicated IdRegistry before writing the joined click to the output log. What failure mode does this ordering introduce, and how do the engineers resolve it?
choices: A joiner may commit the ID to the registry and crash before writing the output, temporarily dropping the click until a background scanner detects the missing output and retries the click
Two joiners may both claim the same ID at once, so the click is billed twice until the advertiser asks for a refund
Claiming first adds a cross-datacentre round trip to every click, so Photon skips the registry for its cheapest ads
items.why: Every click must be registered in the Paxos-backed IdRegistry, which serialises concurrent requests and rejects second claims, preventing double billing. A worker crash between the registry commit and the output write causes temporary undercounting, which the background recovery process resolves to achieve eventual exactness.

summary: **Define correctness requirements before designing the pipeline.** Specify whether windows use event time or processing time, when window outputs trigger, and how the pipeline handles late and duplicate records.

**Every event carries two timestamps.** Event time records when the action occurred at the source, while processing time records when the server ingested the record; network and batching delays create skew between them.
**Aggregate billing metrics by event time.** Windowing by processing time turns a temporary network backlog into an artificial traffic spike when the backlog drains.

**A watermark tracks the progress of event time.** When the watermark timestamp passes a window's end boundary, the pipeline emits the window's count; any record for that window arriving afterwards is classified as late.

**Watermark delay trades output latency against completeness.** Combining a short watermark delay with window revisions delivers low-latency initial counts that converge to exact totals for arrivals within the allowed lateness threshold.

**Unreliable networks cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery, so pipelines implement exactly-once effects.** Assign a unique ID to each event at the client source, then deduplicate against a state store or perform idempotent writes.

**Photon deduplicated clicks across datacentres using a Paxos-replicated IdRegistry.** Active-active pipelines in multiple datacentres processed every click, and the consensus registry ensured only the first joiner to claim a click ID emitted a billing record.

**Probabilistic sketches bound memory usage for high-cardinality aggregations.** A count-min sketch estimates item frequencies with a bounded overestimation error; HyperLogLog estimates distinct item counts within ~2% error using 1.5 KB of memory.

**Log replay can replace a separate batch pipeline.** When a streaming job uses event-time windows and ID deduplication, replaying historical data from a long-retention log through updated code produces deterministic results.

photon.title: Photon's production metrics
photon.text: The SIGMOD 2013 paper reports peak production throughput in the millions of joined events per minute, with an average end-to-end latency from click occurrence to joined billing output of under 10 seconds. Photon's IdRegistry retained click IDs for the preceding N days (typically 3 to 7 days), allowing the system to filter out any duplicate click arriving within that retention window.

watermark.title: Perfect and heuristic watermarks
watermark.text: A bounded or static data source whose timestamps are completely known in advance, such as a closed set of log files, can emit a perfect watermark that never underestimates late data. Open distributed sources, such as mobile devices over cellular networks, can only support heuristic watermarks estimated from network lag distributions. The 2015 Dataflow paper also formalised triggers, which are rules specifying when a window emits results (for example, when the watermark passes, periodically every 1 minute of processing time, or upon every late arrival) and accumulation modes that determine whether revised outputs overwrite or increment previous emissions.

gap.title: At-most-once to exactly-once
gap.text: The Photon authors define their consistency guarantee in three stages: at-most-once billing at any point in time, near-exact completeness within seconds, and exactly-once completeness eventually. In advertising billing, this asymmetry is deliberate: delaying a charge by a few minutes during crash recovery is acceptable, whereas overcharging an advertiser is a critical failure.

hll.title: Coins and leading zeros
hll.text: If you repeatedly flip a fair coin until it lands heads, a run of k consecutive tails before the first heads occurs with probability 2^(-k), or roughly once every 2^k trials. Observing a maximum run of 9 tails suggests you have performed roughly 512 trials. HyperLogLog applies this principle by hashing each item into a uniform pseudo-random bit string and measuring the run of leading zero bits before the first 1 bit. To prevent a single outlier hash from skewing the estimate, the algorithm partitions the stream into m = 2^b buckets using the first b bits of the hash, tracks the maximum leading-zero run in each bucket, and computes the harmonic mean across all m buckets. The standard error of the resulting cardinality estimate is approximately 1.04 / √m. Redis implements HyperLogLog natively using 16,384 buckets (b = 14) of 6-bit registers, occupying 12 KB of memory to achieve a standard error of 0.81%.
